content.title: About
content.content: Dried persimmon is made from fully ripe persimmon fruits (Diospyros kaki) that are peeled and dehydrated until the moisture content drops, preserving most of the fruit’s nutrients. The result is a sweet, slightly caramel‑like flavor with a soft, chewy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Persimmon originates from East Asia but is now cultivated in the Mediterranean, the United States and South America.
In Japan dried persimmon, called “hosho,” is traditionally served during tea ceremonies.
Drying concentrates the natural sugars, making dried persimmon sweeter than the fresh fruit.
The orange hue comes from high levels of carotenoids.
Dried persimmon has been used for centuries in Asian desserts and as a natural sweetener.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Provides essential minerals
items.content: Persimmon supplies potassium, magnesium and iron, important for heart health and blood formation.

items.title: Moderate glycemic impact
items.content: When dried, the fruit raises blood sugar more slowly than many other sweet snacks, making it a reasonable option for controlled carbohydrate intake.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Dried persimmon is calorie‑dense and can spike blood glucose if eaten in large amounts.

items.title: Allergy potential
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to persimmon.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large servings may cause bloating due to the fruit’s fiber load.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy dried persimmon as a snack, toss it into oatmeal, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or use it to make sauces and jams. Soaking it briefly in warm water can re‑hydrate the pieces for a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried persimmon in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator, where it stays fresh for up to 12 months. Discard any pieces that develop mold or off‑odors.
